newsitem.title: INDIA: Cotton-India to launch mission to boost output.
newsitem.headline: Cotton-India to launch mission to boost output.

text.p: India will soon launch a technology mission for cotton to boost production and ensure effective marketing, a top official of the textile ministry said on Thursday.
"There is scope to boost production of cotton by five to six million bales ," Textile Commissioner B.C. Khatua told Reuters. (One bale is 170 kg).
Khatua said the technology mission comprised four mini-missions, covering research, extension work, marketing and processing.

He said India's cotton productivity was around 300 kg per hectare, which was very low compared to the world average of 570 kg and that of some countries like Australia whose output reached 1,200/1,300 kg per hectare.

India's area under cotton cultivation is about 9.0 million hectares, the largest among cotton-producing countries. Nearly 70 percent of the land under cotton cultivation depends on rainfall and the rest is irrigated.
"We only need to step up productivity by about 50 kg per hectare to push up production by five to six million bales and ensure an export of two to three million bales," Khatua said.
He said India at present exported cotton only when it had a surplus.
Extension work and farmers' education in seed, fertiliser and water management formed an important objective of the technology mission, Khatua said.
"Even in Punjab, where irrigation facilities are available, the yield is only 450 kg while in neighbouring Pakistan it is about 700-800 kg," he said.
"The mission should achieve its objectives during the ninth five-year plan (1997-2002)," Khatua said.
A national conference of cotton trade organisations at the weekend estimated the 1996/97 (October/September) cotton crop at a record 16.78 million bales, up from the previous year's 16.27 million.
Cotton prices have been rising despite a record crop in the current season with traders attributing it to a shortage of ready stock.
Dealers said most of the current season's crop had already arrived in the market.
"Whatever is left with farmers will also come into the market with the onset of monsoon this month," said Chandulal Thakkar, a leading cotton dealer.
The four-month June-September monsoon arrived in the southern state of Kerala after a week's delay.

In the week to Thursday, Bengal-deshi rose five rupees to 1,050/1,080 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) and Punjab saw-ginnned by 20 rupees to 1,850/1,900 rupees per maund. F-414 gained 20 rupees to 2,060/2,080 rupees per maund.
Among the Gujarat varieties, Kalyan cotton rose 200 rupees to 14,500/15,000 rupees per candy (355.56 kg). Wagad cotton gained 300 rupees to 13,400 per cenady.
The Indian government last week permitted a state-run agency to export 100,000 bales of cotton.
"The move to export cotton had helped prices further firm," Thakkar said.
